papers.title: Immunopathogenesis of vascular leakage in hantavirus infections: a systematic review of mechanisms underlying HPS and HFRS
papers.abstract: Hantavirus infections manifest as Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS) and Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), both associated with increased vascular permeability despite the lack of direct cytopathic injury to endothelial cells. A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science (January 2020–May 2026) identified human studies investigating immunopathogenic mechanisms in HPS or HFRS. Due to substantial heterogeneity across study designs, findings were synthesized descriptively. Forty-one studies (39 cohorts, 2 case–control) were included, predominantly on HFRS-associated hantaviruses (HTNV, PUUV, DOBV); only one study evaluated HPS-associated ANDV. The reviewed literature revealed elevated inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-18, CXCL10, CX3CL1), depletion of Mucosal-Associated Invariant T (MAIT) cells linked to IRE1αdependent pyroptosis, disruption of the endothelial glycocalyx, and coagulation disturbances with platelet dysfunction. Biomarkers of glycocalyx injury (heparan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate, and soluble thrombomodulin) were associated with increased mortality risk (AUC 0.87–0.93). No human mechanistic studies on Sin Nombre virus (SNV) were identified. Hantavirus-induced vascular leakage is driven by cytokine-mediated endothelial dysfunction, MAIT cell pyroptosis, glycocalyx degradation, and immunothrombosis. While HFRS mechanisms are now well-characterized, the absence of human mechanistic data for HPS—particularly for SNV—remains a critical gap.

A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science (January 2020–May 2026) identified human studies investigating immunopathogenic mechanisms in HPS or HFRS. Due to substantial heterogeneity across study designs, findings were synthesized descriptively. Forty-one studies (39 cohorts, 2 case–control) were included, predominantly on HFRS-associated hantaviruses (HTNV, PUUV, DOBV); only one study evaluated HPS-associated ANDV. The reviewed literature revealed elevated inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-18, CXCL10, CX3CL1), depletion of Mucosal-Associated Invariant T (MAIT) cells linked to IRE1αdependent pyroptosis, disruption of the endothelial glycocalyx, and coagulation disturbances with platelet dysfunction. Biomarkers of glycocalyx injury (heparan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate, and soluble thrombomodulin) were associated with increased mortality risk (AUC 0.87–0.93). No human mechanistic studies on Sin Nombre virus (SNV) were identified. Hantavirus-induced vascular leakage is driven by cytokine-mediated endothelial dysfunction, MAIT cell pyroptosis, glycocalyx degradation, and immunothrombosis. While HFRS mechanisms are now well-characterized, the absence of human mechanistic data for HPS—particularly for SNV—remains a critical gap.

analysis.background: Hantavirus infections cause HPS and HFRS, both marked by vascular leakage without direct endothelial cytopathy.
analysis.main_directions: The review synthesizes human studies on cytokine storms, MAIT cell pyroptosis, glycocalyx disruption, and coagulation abnormalities driving leakage.
analysis.current_state: Most evidence comes from HFRS hantaviruses (HTNV, PUUV, DOBV); only one HPS study on ANDV exists, with glycocalyx biomarkers linked to mortality (AUC 0.87–0.93).
analysis.gaps: No human mechanistic data exist for HPS-associated SNV, and overall HPS studies are sparse.
analysis.future_research: Future work should target human mechanistic studies of HPS, especially SNV, to clarify cytokine, glycocalyx, and immunothrombosis pathways.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infections cause HPS and HFRS, both marked by vascular leakage without direct endothelial cytopathy. Main directions: The review synthesizes human studies on cytokine storms, MAIT cell pyroptosis, glycocalyx disruption, and coagulation abnormalities driving leakage. Current state: Most evidence comes from HFRS hantaviruses (HTNV, PUUV, DOBV); only one HPS study on ANDV exists, with glycocalyx biomarkers linked to mortality (AUC 0.87–0.93). Gaps: No human mechanistic data exist for HPS-associated SNV, and overall HPS studies are sparse. Future research: Future work should target human mechanistic studies of HPS, especially SNV, to clarify cytokine, glycocalyx, and immunothrombosis pathways.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 感染导致血管渗漏的免疫发病机制:针对 HPS 与 HFRS 机制的系统综述

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 感染导致汉坦病毒肺综合征和肾综合征出血热,两者均表现为血管渗漏而无直接内皮细胞病变。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 该综述综合了人类研究,涉及细胞因子风暴、MAIT细胞焦亡、糖萼破坏以及凝血异常导致渗漏的机制。
analysis_zh.current_state: 大部分证据来自肾综合征出血热 汉坦病毒es(HTNV、PUUV、DOBV);仅有一项关于安第斯病毒(ANDV)的汉坦病毒肺综合征(HPS)研究,发现糖萼生物标志物与死亡率相关(AUC 0.87–0.93)。
analysis_zh.gaps: 目前尚无关于汉坦病毒肺综合征相关SNV的人体机制数据,且整体HPS研究稀缺。
analysis_zh.future_research: 未来工作应聚焦于汉坦病毒肺综合征,特别是SNV的人体机制研究,以阐明细胞因子、糖萼及免疫血栓形成通路。

papers.title: Revisiting Animal Reservoirs of Hantavirus and Other Zoonotic Viruses Associated with Cruise Travel: Impact and Prevention.
papers.abstract: The sustained growth of international maritime tourism and the expansion of the cruise industry have increased the importance of emerging zoonotic diseases as a significant challenge to global public health. Cruise ships constitute complex epidemiological settings characterized by high population density, rapid international mobility, and constant interaction between humans, animals, and coastal environments, factors that favor the introduction and spread of emerging infectious agents. Potential zoonotic concerns include orthohantaviruses and other zoonotic viruses, such as dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever, and avian influenza, which are associated with animal reservoirs and vectors in ports, tourist destinations, and tropical ecosystems. This review examines the ecology of animal reservoirs of orthohantaviruses and other zoonotic pathogens relevant to maritime tourism, including peri-urban rodents, bats, migratory birds, and other mammals. It discusses how climate change, coastal urbanization, and environmental change affect viral transmission dynamics. It highlights epidemiological risks linked to international cruises, particularly exposure during ecotourism excursions, pathogen introduction, and challenges for maritime surveillance. The review also addresses travel medicine, biosecurity, and infection control, emphasizing a One Health approach. Strengthening integrated surveillance and prevention systems is essential to ensure safer, more sustainable, and resilient maritime tourism in the 21st century.

full_text_sections.full_text: Revisiting Animal Reservoirs of Hantavirus and Other Zoonotic Viruses Associated with Cruise Travel: Impact and Prevention - PMID: 42791822 - DOI: 10.3390/ani16182966 Revisiting Animal Reservoirs of Hantavirus and Other Zoonotic Viruses Associated with Cruise Travel: Impact and Prevention Abstract The sustained growth of international maritime tourism and the expansion of the cruise industry have increased the importance of emerging zoonotic diseases as a significant challenge to global public health. Cruise ships constitute complex epidemiological settings characterized by high population density, rapid international mobility, and constant interaction between humans, animals, and coastal environments, factors that favor the introduction and spread of emerging infectious agents. Potential zoonotic concerns include orthohantaviruses and other zoonotic viruses, such as dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever, and avian influenza, which are associated with animal reservoirs and vectors in ports, tourist destinations, and tropical ecosystems. This review examines the ecology of animal reservoirs of orthohantaviruses and other zoonotic pathogens relevant to maritime tourism, including peri-urban rodents, bats, migratory birds, and other mammals. It discusses how climate change, coastal urbanization, and environmental change affect viral transmission dynamics. It highlights epidemiological risks linked to international cruises, particularly exposure during ecotourism excursions, pathogen introduction, and challenges for maritime surveillance. The review also addresses travel medicine, biosecurity, and infection control, emphasizing a One Health approach. Strengthening integrated surveillance and prevention systems is essential to ensure safer, more sustainable, and resilient maritime tourism in the 21st century. Keywords: international cruises; one health; orthohantavirus; travel medicine; viral zoonoses. Publication types Grants and funding LinkOut - more resources - Full Text Sources

papers.title: Differences in Ecological Drivers for Leptospira and Hantavirus in an Urban Norway Rat Population.
papers.abstract: Rodent control in urban areas is an important public health measure, among other reasons, for their capacity of harboring several zoonotic pathogens. Efficient, evidence-based control programs must consider both rodent and pathogen ecology, to achieve both rodent population and pathogen transmission risk reduction. The present study aims to determine the ecological drivers of Leptospira and Hantavirus positivity in an urban Norway Rat population. One hundred and twenty rats were trapped in four urban poor communities in Salvador, Brazil, tested for Leptospira sp. and Hantavirus. Generalized Linear Models for Leptospira (N=109) and Hantavirus (N=108) positivity were created with a pool of environmental and demographic variables, followed by stepwise model selection using Akaike's Information Criterion. Age, presence of Calodium hepaticum scars, wounds, accumulated materials, open sewer canals and unpaved soil were positively associated with Leptospira positivity. Age and presence of accumulated materials were positively associated with Hantavirus positivity, while rodent control campaigns and being male were protective factors. Factors associated with positivity for Leptospira are also associated with rodent infestation. Different subsets of environmental and demographic factors influence pathogens with different epidemiological characteristics. Control measures that effectively reduce zoonotic risk must consider the ecological characteristics of the pathogens present in the system.
authors: Ana Maria Borges da Paixão Barreto

Currently, rats are almost exclusively associated with human occupation, often of urbanized areas, are significantly dependent on the re- sources made available by human activity (Feng and Himsworth 2013). The relationship between rats and humans is not harmonious, with rats being considered pests, causing damage to farming and infrastructure, and contaminating food stocks (Jacob and Buckle 2018). Estimations suggest, conservatively, that the Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus, alone causes economic damage of more than USD 30 million/ year globally (Diagne et al. 2023). Throughout the Global South, the fast growth of urban centers often results in the creation of informal settlements, characterized by deficiencies in the provision and coverage of basic urban services (e.g., trash collection, sanitation, pest control) and infrastructure (Carvalho-Pereira et al. 2024; Costa et al. 2014; de Oliveira et al. 2024). The resulting environment is highly conductive to rodent infestation, with an abundance of water, food and shelter (Panti-May et al. 2016). Such close coexistence exposes the populations of the settlements to the pathogens carried by rats (Costa, Ribeiro, et al. 2014; Muschetto et al. 2025). The role of rats as a zoonotic pathogen reservoir is arguably one of the most impactful threats posed by our proximity. Rodents host a remarkable diversity of zoonotic pathogens, including viruses, bacteria, unicellular eukary- ote and helminth parasites (Luis et al. 2013; Himsworth et al. 2013; Delaney, Treuting, and Rothenburger 2018). Some of the most historically relevant pathogens have ro- dents as their reservoir, such as Yersinia pestis (Rahelinirina et al. 2021), Leptospira sp. (A. Minter et al. 2017) and Hantavirus (Dearing and Dizney 2010). Depending on the pathogen, rodents can either be direct sources of infection or act as part of the transmission cycle, shedding bacteria to the environment or promoting infective contact with competent hosts that thus infect humans (Himsworth et al. 2013). Important examples of pathogens carried by Norway rats are Leptospira spp. (Feng and Himsworth 2013), Hantavirus (Chen et al. 2023), and Toxoplasma gondii (Bazan et al. 2025). With over one million estimated human cases per year (Costa et al. 2015), the infection can cause asymptomatic/mild forms or evolve into severe and potentially lethal forms such as Weil’s disease and Leptospirosis-associated pulmonary hemor- rhage syndrome (Ko, Goarant, and Picardeau 2009). In Salvador, leptospirosis is a long-standing challenge to public health in impoverished urban communities (Ko et al. 1999; Ribeiro et al. 2008). Norway rats are the main reservoirs of Orthohantavirus seoulense, with chronic, nearly asymptomatic infection (Jonsson et al.2010; Meyer and Schmaljohn 2000). SEOV is considered to be cosmopolitan following the worldwide distribution of rats (Himsworth et al. 2013) and has been previously detected in rats in Salvador (Costa et al. 2014). Toxoplasma gondii is an apicomplexan parasite that widely infects warm-blooded animals, causing grave illness in immunocompromised individuals, as well as fetal development issues through congenital toxoplasmosis (S.G. C. G. Zeppelini et al. Sanchez and Besteiro 2021). While important for the epi- demiology of toxoplasmosis, infection by T. gondii in rats causes behavioral changes, but limited health effects (Ruf- folo et al. 2016; Webster 1994). For the control of rat-borne zoonoses, the ecology of the zoonotic system should also be considered, as this presents its own ecological characteristics (Caio et al. 2016), an important consideration given the diversity of patho- gens that rats can carry, including potential coinfections (Carvalho-Pereira et al. 2018; Costa et al. 2014; L.K.F. Lee et al. 2023). Previous studies in urban informal settlements in Salvador have investigated urban rodent ecology (Panti- May et al. 2016; C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021; Eyre et al. 2020), movement (Awoniyi et al. 2021), the parasites and pathogens they carry (Costa, Porter, et al. 2014; Carvalho- Pereira et al. 2018), and the impacts of infestation on hu- man health (Costa, Ribeiro, et al. 2014; Costa et al. 2021). However, studies have focused on isolated pathogens (Souza et al. 2021; Bazan et al. 2025; Pimentel Sobrinho et al. 2020), not yet evaluating potential ecological inter- actions between these pathogens, such as how environ- mental and demographic factors might differ between them. Knowledge of pathogen ecology of Norway rats, a multi-pathogen reservoir, including prevalence and pa- thogen characteristics and the impacts of environmental factors on their dynamics is essential to lead to targeted control and intervention strategies. Different pathogens can present different characteristics (e.g., acquisition route, tissue tropism, requirements for transmission) even if infecting the same host species, likely resulting in different responses to control measures. Our study aims to quantify zoonotic positivity for three different pathogens (Hantavirus, Leptospira spp. and Toxoplasma gondii) in Norway rats from urban impover- ished communities in the city of Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, and identify whether the ecological processes that drive rat infection risk vary between pathogens. Characterizing zoonotic spillover risk in rodents and identifying environ- mental risk factors is fundamental for the development of rodent-borne zoonosis control programs that are resilient against the risk of pathogen (re)emergence as an unpre- dicted negative effect of the control program itself. MATERIALS AND METHODS Ethical Statement Rodent sampling and biological sample harvesting proce- dures were authorized under license from the Ethics Committee for Animal Use of Fiocruz Bahia (authorization #019/2016). The study was conducted and reported fol- lowing ARRIVE guidelines. Study Site The city of Salvador, Bahia (12 550 28.03‘‘ S, 38 280 34.900 W) is one of the largest urban centers in Brazil, with 692,819 km2 and over 2.5 million inhabitants, 42.7% of which living in informal settlements (henceforth commu- nities) (IBGE 2022, 2015). Four communities were sam- pled: Marechal Rondon (MR), Alto do Cabrito (AC), Rio Sena (RS) e Nova Constituinte (NC), selected for their location in the same sanitary district (subdivisions of the city’s territory used for the operations of health authorities, including the Zoonosis Control Center [CCZ]), reflecting their sociodemographic similarity and environmental pro- file, which fit the criteria for classification as slums (inad- equate housing conditions, limited or absent access to safe drinking water and sanitation), (Economic and Affairs 2019), and lack of adequate solid waste collection (in- cluding formation of open trash piles). All four commu- nities were set on hills, with small natural waterways running at their lowermost point, which receive the com- munities’ household sewage. According to the CCZ, the communities have chronic issues with rodent infestation. In each community, the study area was defined as a poly- gon of 0.07–0.09 km2. Zoonotic Positivity for Rattus Norvegicus Rat capture data, and environmental and biological sam- ples (kidney imprints, urine, blood and brain matter) were obtained from a previous field sampling study conducted in four communities, performed in two campaigns (40 semi- randomized trapping points with two Tomahawk-type traps, 4 trap-nights per campaign, April-June and October– November 2018) (C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021). During necropsy and tissue sample harvesting, the presence of Calodium hepaticum (a helminth species that parasitises the liver of mammals, frequently observed in wild Rattus) was registered during the examination of the liver. The presence Differences in Ecological Drivers for Leptospira and Hantavirus of the characteristic scars in the liver cortex was considered as a positive detection for the individual (Fuehrer 2014). Positivity for Leptospira was assessed by a combination of Indirect Fluorescent Antibody (IFA) assays performed on Poli-L-Lysine-treated microscope slides with kidney imprints (D et al. 2016) and/or urine sample qPCR tar- geting the lipL32 gene as previously described (Costa, Wunder, et al. 2015). Hantavirus positivity was determined by Enzyme-linked Immunoassay (ELISA) tests, using orthohantavirus purified recombinant nucleoprotein as antigen (Padula et al. 2000). Detection of Toxoplasma was performed through nested-PCR tests targeting the IST1 region of T. gondii (Hurtado et al. 2001). Due to limitations in availability, PCR tests for Hantavirus (RT-PCR targeting the Hantavirus-specific RNA-dependent RNA polymerase- encoding L segment) were restricted to ELISA-positive rats. All PCR tests were negative. The physical condition of rats was measured as a weight-length ratio that took into account the effect of age (Peig and Green 2009). Age of individuals was calculated in days based in morphometric data following the von Ber- talanffy equation, with parameters obtained by fitting data derived from the growth curve for male rats (Calhoun 1962; Burthe et al. 2009). Morphology data, presence of parasites and of wounds were obtained during animal processing (C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021). Environmental Variables A standardized descriptive questionnaire was applied to obtain the environmental data used to characterize the environment at each sampling point. The data collection occurred at the moment of trapping, being performed considering a 20-m-radius buffer around the sampling point (C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021). Variables describe the presence of other animals, human-made materials (refuse, construction materials, debris), soil condition and presence of water, as well as rodent control activities (both carried by the locals themselves and by the Zoonosis Control Center) in the region at the moment the traps were set. Data on opossum presence were derived from captures during the trapping period. Data on presence of animals and rodent control measures in the trapping area (i.e., household backyards) were voluntarily provided by the resident dur- ing trap setting. Variables collected are listed in Table 1. Statistical Analysis To evaluate each outcome (positivity for Leptospira, Tox- oplasma, or Hantavirus), a set of variables was defined based on hypotheses that link the biological processes known to be relevant to each pathogen to the outcome (Table 1). Positivity for the other pathogens was also added as a variable to evaluate if coinfection affects the chances of positivity for each zoonotic pathogen. Collinearity was verified through the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF), with variables having a VIF under 5 considered apt to compose the variable pool for each outcome. Generalized linear models (GLMs) were performed for each outcome using the VIF-verified and hypothesis-associated variables, fol- lowed by backwards stepwise model selection based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). Models were consid- ered plausible when DAIC < 2 compared to the model with the lowest AIC and selected based on maximum parsimony (lowest DAIC and number of variables). All analyses were performed using the packages Tidyverse, lme4 e MuMIn, on R Core Team, 2026 (Wickham et al. 2019; Bates et al. 2015; Barton 2022). Due to the low positivity for Toxoplasma, only Hantavirus and Leptospira were analysed by GLM and model selection. The model for Leptospira was performed with 109 individuals (7 individuals removed due to incomplete associated data), with this subset presenting 48.6% (53/ 109) positivity, and 108 individuals were employed for the Hantavirus model (9 individuals removed due to incom- plete data), presenting 33.3% (36/108) positivity. From the subsets with complete data, 39.6% (21/53) of the Lep- tospira-positive rats were also positive for Hantavirus, while 58.3% (21/36) of orthohantavirus-positive rats were also positive for Leptospira. analysis.summary_en: Background: Rodent control is a key public health measure because rats harbor many zoonotic pathogens. Methods: 120 Norway rats were trapped in four urban poor communities in Salvador, Brazil; Leptospira and Hantavirus status were tested and GLMs were built with environmental and demographic variables (N=109 for Leptospira, N=108 for Hantavirus). papers.title: Hantavirus RNA Detection in Small Mammals and Spatial Association with Human Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome in the West Kazakhstan Region, 2025
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease associated with orthohantaviruses maintained in natural rodent hosts. This study assessed the detection and spatial distribution of hantavirus RNA among small mammals in the West Kazakhstan Region in 2025 and compared rodent surveillance findings with human HFRS occurrence. An observational descriptive-analytical study was conducted in August–September 2025 in four districts. A total of 343 small mammals were captured and morphologically identified. Lung tissues were tested using 123 pooled testing units, while 14 specimens were tested individually during the same surveillance campaign. Thus, 137 testing units representing 343 animals were evaluated by real-time and conventional RT-PCR. The minimum infection rate (MIR) was calculated as a descriptive minimum estimate, and a pooled-testing likelihood model was used to account for variation in testing-unit size. Hantavirus RNA was detected in 47/137 testing units, including 45 positive pooled units and two individually positive specimens, corresponding to a descriptive MIR of 13.7%. The model-based individual-level infection probability was estimated at 18.0% (95% profile-likelihood CI: 13.5–23.1%). Positive testing units were observed among Apodemus uralensis, Myodes glareolus, and Microtus arvalis. At the district level, the descriptive MIR ranged from 11.6% in Burlinsky to 19.0% in Chingirlauisky. Sampling sites overlapped spatially with settlements reporting human HFRS cases, including Utvinka, Daryinsk, and Rubezhinskoye; however, spatial coincidence does not establish direct transmission.

analysis.background: HFRS is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses maintained in rodent hosts (A1).
analysis.methods: An observational descriptive‑analytical study was performed in August–September 2025 across four districts of West Kazakhstan (A3, A2). A total of 343 small mammals were captured and morphologically identified (A4). Lung tissues were tested in 123 pooled units and 14 individual specimens, yielding 137 testing units evaluated by real‑time and conventional RT‑PCR (A5, A6).
analysis.results: Hantavirus RNA was found in 47 of 137 testing units, giving a descriptive MIR of 13.7% (A8); a model‑based individual infection probability was 18.0% (95% CI 13.5–23.1%) (A9). Positive units occurred in Apodemus uralensis, Myodes glareolus, and Microtus arvalis (A10) and MIR varied by district from 11.6% to 19.0% (A11). Sampling sites overlapped settlements with human HFRS cases, though spatial coincidence does not prove direct transmission (A12, A13).
analysis.contribution: The study provides surveillance data linking rodent hantavirus prevalence to human HFRS occurrence and highlights spatial overlap that can inform public‑health risk mapping (A2, A12).
analysis.limitations: Only abstract data are available, limiting detail on methods and sample representativeness; spatial overlap alone cannot establish causation (A13, evidence_scope).

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a rodent‑borne zoonosis caused by orthohantaviruses (A1). Methods: An observational descriptive‑analytical survey in four West Kazakhstan districts (Aug‑Sep 2025) captured 343 small mammals, whose lung tissues were tested in 137 pooled/individual RT‑PCR units (A3‑A6). Results: Hantavirus RNA was detected in 47/137 units (MIR 13.7%); model‑based infection probability 18.0% (95% CI 13.5–23.1%) (A8‑A9). Positive species included Apodemus uralensis, Myodes glareolus, Microtus arvalis, with district MIR 11.6–19.0% (A10‑A11). Sampling sites overlapped human HFRS settlements, but spatial coincidence does not prove transmission (A12‑A13). Contribution: Provides rodent surveillance linked to human cases, aiding risk mapping (A2, A12). Limitations: Abstract‑only data; spatial overlap cannot infer causation (A13).

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 RNA 检测在小型哺乳动物中,并与人类 肾综合征出血热 的空间关联,位于哈萨克斯坦西部地区,2025年

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热是一种人畜共患疾病,由 正汉坦病毒 在啮齿动物宿主中维持(A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 在2025年8–9月于哈萨克斯坦西部四个地区(A3,A2)开展了一项观察性描述性-分析性研究。共捕获并形态学鉴定了343只小型哺乳动物(A4)。对123个混合样本和14个单独标本的肺组织进行检测,形成共137个检测单元,采用实时和常规RT‐PCR进行检测(A5,A6)。
analysis_zh.results: 汉坦病毒 RNA在137个检测单元中有47个检测阳性,描述性最低感染率(MIR)为13.7%(A8);基于模型的单个感染概率为18.0%(95% CI 13.5–23.1%)(A9)。阳性单元出现在乌拉尔田鼠(Apodemus uralensis)、灰田鼠(Myodes glareolus)和田野田鼠(Microtus arvalis)(A10),各地区的MIR在11.6%至19.0%之间变化(A11)。采样地点与有人类肾综合征出血热病例的定居点重叠,尽管空间重合并不证明直接传播(A12,A13)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究提供了将啮齿动物 汉坦病毒 流行率与人类肾综合征出血热发生关联的监测数据,并强调空间重叠,可用于公共卫生风险绘图(A2,A12)。

papers.title: Multi-omics Reveals Divergent Endothelial Molecular Responses to New and Old World Hantaviruses.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses cause vascular leakage syndromes that vary in clinical manifestation and severity. Although tissue tropism contributes to these differences, both Old and New World hantaviruses infect endothelial cells, where species-specific disease phenotypes remain poorly understood. Here we integrated time-resolved global RNA sequencing, mass spectrometry proteomics, and phosphoproteomics of human endothelial cells infected with New World Andes virus (ANDV) or Old World Hantaan virus (HTNV). Despite equivalent early viral RNA and protein levels, ANDV elicited a stronger innate immune protein response, preceding its restriction while HTNV replication continued. At later stages of infection, HTNV induced downregulation of cytoskeletal and junctional protein phosphorylation, accompanied by visual disruption of cellular actin architecture. Additionally, ANDV induced heightened activity of ERBB-family kinases, whose chemical inhibition by neratinib and afatinib reduced viral replication. Together, these data define species-specific responses in endothelial cells, identify druggable host targets, and reveal mechanisms with relevance to divergent vascular leakage symptomology.
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause vascular leakage syndromes with variable severity and infect endothelial cells, but species‑specific mechanisms are unclear. papers.title: Habitat-Mediated Spillover Risk of Andes Hantavirus in Oligoryzomys longicaudatus: A Mechanistic Eco-Epidemiological Model.
papers.abstract: Andes hantavirus (ANDV) is a rodent-borne orthohantavirus associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in southern South America. Its maintenance and spillover risk depend on the ecology of its principal reservoir, Oligoryzomys longicaudatus, and on environmental changes that alter habitat availability, host abundance, and human-rodent interfaces. We developed a mechanistic eco-epidemiological model that couples effective habitat cover to an SIR framework for ANDV transmission in O. longicaudatus. Habitat degradation and compensatory restoration modify rodent carrying capacity, natality, and the force of infection, which depends on infected host load relative to instantaneous ecological capacity. We derived the habitat equilibrium, the basic reproduction number R0, and the time-dependent effective reproduction number Re(t) and evaluated infection-burden and threshold indicators across degradation-restoration scenarios. The analysis shows that R0 is independent of equilibrium habitat cover because susceptible abundance scales with carrying capacity at the disease-free equilibrium. In contrast, Re(t), cumulative incidence, and infected load depend on transient habitat-mediated crowding. Restoration increases reservoir abundance and absolute infection burden, whereas degradation can reduce abundance while increasing crowding-driven transmission pressure and prolonging supercritical windows. These results identify ecological conditions under which habitat change may intensify reservoir infection pressure and guide One Health surveillance at human-rodent interfaces.

papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒 [PDI0109] (ANDV) 在长尾鼠 Oligoryzomys longicaudatus 中的栖息地介导跨种传播风险:一种机制生态流行病学模型。

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒 汉坦病毒(ANDV)是一种由啮齿动物传播的 正汉坦病毒,在南美洲南部导致 汉坦病毒心肺综合征;其维持和溢出风险取决于其主要宿主 Oligoryzomys longicaudatus 的生态以及改变宿主丰度和人-啮齿动物接口的栖息地变化。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者开发了一种将有效栖息地覆盖率与 Oligoryzomys longicaudatus 中安第斯病毒(ANDV)传播的 SIR 框架耦合的机制性生态流行病学模型,纳入了栖息地介导的承载力、出生率和感染力的影响,并推导了栖息地平衡、基本再生数 R0 以及在退化-恢复情景下的时间依赖有效再生数 Re(t)。
analysis_zh.results: 分析表明,R0 与平衡栖息地覆盖率无关,因为易感个体数量随疾病自由平衡时的承载力而缩放;相反,Re(t)、累计发病率和感染负荷取决于瞬态栖息地介导的拥挤;恢复可增加宿主丰度和绝对感染负担,而退化则可能降低丰度但增加拥挤驱动的传播压力并延长超临界窗口。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些结果明确了栖息地变化可能加剧宿主感染压力的生态条件,并为人畜接口的 One Health 监测提供指导。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供了摘要;未在所提供证据中报告具体数据、验证和详细局限性。

papers.title: AI-generated medical realism and hantavirus misinformation: a new public health threat?
papers.abstract: The widespread availability of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has substantially reshaped the health-information environment compared with the COVID-19 pandemic. Contemporary AI tools can rapidly generate highly realistic medical-looking content from text, including laboratory reports, radiological images, histological slides, and institutional clinical documentation. During infectious disease outbreaks, such simulated medical content may exploit the visual authority traditionally associated with healthcare institutions and influence public risk perception. During media coverage of the May 2026 Andes virus (ANDV) alert in Italy, news outlets published realistic AI-generated medical imagery depicting hantavirus diagnostic reports, hospital-associated laboratory materials, and outbreak-response scenes linked to real healthcare institutions. One image, in particular, reproduced the visual identity of a real laboratory report produced at "Luigi Sacco" University Hospital despite displaying multiple inconsistencies. In some additional examples, AI generation was not clearly disclosed despite the use of recognizable institutional names and logos. This phenomenon has the potential to extend beyond isolated misinformation events. Emerging evidence indicates that experts may struggle to reliably distinguish AI-generated biomedical and radiological images from authentic materials, raising concern that future infectious disease outbreaks may occur within an information ecosystem increasingly shaped by visually persuasive synthetic media. Such content may amplify public anxiety, distort perceptions of authority, and erode trust in institutions. Synthetic medical realism should therefore be considered a potential emerging category of public-health risk during infectious disease emergencies that requires coordinated action from institutions and regulators developing verification systems, while news media, platforms, and publishers implement AI-disclosure standards and guidelines for synthetic biomedical content.

papers.title: Generation and Characterization of the Human Anti-HTNV Antibody KJJ4.
papers.abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is the predominant causative agent of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in China, yet no specific antiviral therapy is currently available. Neutralizing antibodies (NAbs) represent a promising strategy, but most existing anti-HTNV NAbs are heterologous and carry immunogenicity risks. Here, two fully human antibodies from a previously established human anti-HTNV phage display library were generated and characterized. KJJ3, a VL-VL tandem antibody derived from clone 3-12, showed weak binding to inactivated HTNV and minimal neutralizing activity (IC50 = 27.12 μg/mL). However, KJJ4, an engineered IgG4 antibody derived from clone 4-19 and carrying the S108P hinge mutation to prevent Fab-arm exchange, bound inactivated HTNV antigen and recombinant glycoprotein Gn (residues 19-371) in a dose-dependent manner, with only weak binding to Gc. Surface plasmon resonance yielded an association rate constant of 4.70 × 103 M-1s-1, a dissociation rate constant of 3.06 × 10-3 s-1, and an equilibrium dissociation constant of 650 nM for monomeric Gn19-371. In a Vero E6 focus-reduction microneutralization assay, KJJ4 neutralized HTNV in vitro with an IC50 of 2.879 μg/mL. These data establish KJJ4 as a fully human anti-HTNV antibody with experimentally defined in vitro binding and neutralizing activity, warranting further evaluation in animal models of HTNV infection.

analysis.background: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is the predominant cause of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in China and no specific antiviral therapy exists.
analysis.methods: Two fully human antibodies were generated from a human anti‑HTNV phage‑display library; KJJ4 was engineered as an IgG4 with an S108P hinge mutation, and its binding to inactivated HTNV, Gn19‑371, and Gc was assessed dose‑dependently, with SPR (ka = 4.70×10^3 M⁻¹s⁻¹, kd = 3.06×10⁻³ s⁻¹, KD = 650 nM) and a Vero E6 focus‑reduction microneutralization assay.

analysis.limitations: Data are limited to abstract‑only in‑vitro findings; no animal‑model or clinical efficacy data are reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HTNV causes HFRS in China and lacks specific antivirals. Methods: Two fully human antibodies were derived from a phage‑display library; KJJ4, an engineered IgG4 with S108P hinge, was characterized by dose‑dependent binding, SPR (ka 4.70×10^3 M⁻¹s⁻¹, kd 3.06×10⁻³ s⁻¹, KD 650 nM) and Vero E6 microneutralization. Contribution: Demonstrates a fully human anti‑HTNV IgG4 with in‑vitro activity, supporting further pre‑clinical work. Limitations: Findings are restricted to abstract‑level in‑vitro data; no animal or clinical data are provided.
